content: Bulletin boards allow users to share and distribute computer programs. Additionally, computer programming texts often include examples of actual code, which programmers are encouraged to copy. Programmers frequently incorporate existing public domain software into their own works. Therefore, courts must carefully limit copyright protection to only those elements of a program that represent the author’s original work. Although the case of Computer Associates only briefly mentioned this issue, Nimmer notes that the public domain is particularly rich and valuable for computer programs. He suggests that a computer program author who wishes to release their work into the public domain can either include it in a book as example code or post it on a bulletin board, encouraging sharing and distribution. (Nimmer is widely regarded as an authoritative source in copyright law.) With respect to patents, public use or publishing the details of an invention before applying for a patent generally places the invention in the public domain and theoretically prevents it from being patented by anyone. For example, publishing a chemical formula in a journal prevents anyone from patenting that formula. This tactic was commonly employed by Bell Labs to establish prior art without the inconvenience, cost, and effort of filing patent applications for inventions of no immediate monetary value. (The UNIX operating system was famously described in such a journal.) This approach is sometimes referred to as defensive disclosure, a strategy to ensure that one is not later accused of infringing a patent on their own invention. Under U.S. law (not European law), an inventor may file a patent claim up to one year after publishing a description, provided no one else has published or used it first. In practice, patent examiners primarily consider other patents and the books available in their library when evaluating prior art. This is due to the patent office’s elaborate classification system for inventions. As a result, an increasing number of issued patents may be invalid because of prior art that was not brought to the examiner’s attention. Once a patent is issued, invalidating it is a very expensive process. Publishing a description on a website as a preemptive disclosure does little in practice to release an invention into the public domain; it might still be considered patentable, albeit erroneously. However, anyone aware of omitted prior art in an issued patent may submit it to the U.S. Patent Office and request a reexamination of the patent during its enforceable period (its life plus the statute of limitations). This process may result in the loss of some or all of the patent’s claims, or it may backfire and actually strengthen the claims. An applicant may also choose to file a Statutory Invention Registration (SIR), which has the same effect as a patent for prior art purposes. These SIRs are relatively expensive and are used strategically by large companies to prevent competitors from obtaining patents. Section 102(c) of U.S. patent law states that an invention that has been abandoned cannot be patented, but there is very little case law on this point, making it largely a dead letter. If an inventor has an issued patent, there are several ways to release it into the public domain other than simply letting it expire. First, the inventor can fail to pay the maintenance fee, which is due approximately every four years. Alternatively, the inventor can file a disclaimer with the U.S. Patent Office, explicitly dedicating the patent to the public. This disclaimer is binding on the patent holder and their successors or assigns. This approach is often used during the application process to prevent another patent from being invalidated due to double patenting. Lastly, the inventor may grant a patent license to the world, although the issue of revocability may arise. Trade secrets, if properly guarded, can last indefinitely. For example, the formula for Coca-Cola has been kept as a trade secret. However, once a trade secret is disclosed to the public, it enters the public domain. Despite this, an invention using the former trade secret may still be patentable in the United States if it is not barred by statute (including the on-sale bar). Some businesses choose to protect products, processes, and information by maintaining them as trade secrets rather than patenting them. For instance, Hershey does not patent some of its processes, such as the recipe for Reese’s, but instead keeps them as trade secrets to prevent competitors from easily duplicating or learning from their disclosures. A trademark registration is renewable indefinitely. If a trademark owner wishes to maintain their registration, they must pay renewal fees, use the trademark, and defend the registration. However, a trademark or brand can become unenforceable if it becomes the generic term for a particular type of product or service, a process known as genericide. When a mark undergoes genericide, people use the term generically rather than as a trademark to exclusively identify the source of a product or service. A well-known example is thermos in the United States. Because trademarks are registered with governments, some countries or trademark registries may recognize a mark, while others may determine that it is generic and not allowable as a trademark in that jurisdiction. For example, the drug acetylsalicylic acid (2-acetoxybenzoic acid) is better known as aspirin in the United States, where it is a generic term. In Canada, however, Aspirin remains a trademark of the German company Bayer. Bayer lost the trademark in the United States after World War I, when the mark was sold to an American firm. The influx of copycat products during the war led to the term being deemed generic just three years later. Terms can be deemed generic in two ways. First, a potential mark can be deemed generic by a trademark registry, which refuses to register it. Second, a registered trademark can become generic through widespread public use as a generic term.
